speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: MR. KNOWLES (WINNIPEG NORTH CENTRE)-ALLEGED DEROGATORY REFERENCE TO PUBLIC SERVICE BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege, notice of which I sent to Your Honour. In Hansard of yesterday, which reached us this morning, a statement is recorded that was made yesterday which I am afraid got lost in the chaos but which in my view constitutes a question of privilege, at least for many of us in this House of Commons. I raise this matter not in any desire to enter into a confrontation but in the hope that it might be resolved quickly. As recorded on page 9805 of Hansard for yesterday, the Prime Minister, in the course of answering a question, said:
If individuals in the Public Service, egged on by the opposition in many cases-
Then there follow about a dozen lines of various interjections, after which the Prime Minister again got the floor and said:
If individuals throughout the Public Service decide to take justice into their own hands and set themselves above those elected to represent the people, I think this is a very serious thing for the country, not for the government.
My point of privilege, sir, is that many of us in this House have been here for many years and if there is one thing that we have learned in Ottawa it is that we have a Public Service than which there is none better. To my knowledge, individuals throughout the Public Service are as loyal as they can be to their ultimate employers, the people of Canada, and in particular to their immediate employer, the government.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: MR. KNOWLES (WINNIPEG NORTH CENTRE)-ALLEGED DEROGATORY REFERENCE TO PUBLIC SERVICE BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Since we in this House have many dealings with the Public Service and since they cannot speak for themselves I think it is a matter of privilege on our part when those in whom we have confidence are maligned in this way. I feel that at the earliest opportunity this statement by the Prime Minister, which was so broad in that he referred to individuals throughout the Public Service, should be corrected. I do not move a motion that it be referred to committee for investigation. I simply make an earnest plea to the Prime
Minister that he now correct the statement he made yesterday.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
That the Fifth Report of the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development, presented to the House, Wednesday, June 30, 1971, be concurred in.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I think what I should probably do at the outset is to make the suggestion that, because the report to which this motion refers is one of great fundamental importance and of great concern not only to the Indian people but to the country generally, Parliament might consider voting on it today. During the course of the debate, if it is not adjourned, perhaps the House leaders might meet and come to some conclusion about a time allocation order so that Parliament can express an opinion with respect to this unanimous report by one of its committees on this subject matter inasmuch as I am sure none of the members of the government would disagree with the opinions expressed in the report.
Within the last few days the subject of educational opportunities and facilities for our native Indian people has been brought into pretty sharp focus. True, it has been a matter of concern to the parliamentary committee that made the report for some two or three years, during which it held extensive hearings, listened to numerous representations and obviously, from the tenor of the content of the report, considered the subject in even greater depth than many committees consider the subject matters that are referred to them. It is also a matter that has been inquired about in the House from time to time since the report was tabled.
Perhaps I might refer to one specific point which helped to bring the question noticeably and pointedly to public attention. I refer to the publicity in which the Indian

Association of Alberta has been involved within the last few days relating to an earlier presentation the association made to the government of Canada, to all parties represented in the House, I believe, and to members of the standing committee. The members of this association made a very worth-while, well thought-out, well documented presentation in March, 1970, seeking to have established an Indian educational and cultural complex in the province of Alberta, operated by and for the benefit of the Indian people in that province. The plan for that complex was a very impressive one and very imaginative.
No member who sat in on any of the meetings or made any examination of the plan had anything but the highest of praise for the concepts behind it. It reflected the concern and the depth of feeling that only a group of people can have about themselves. It reflected a depth of feeling that only a group of people can show when they are intimately concerned about their own well-being and their own future. I think we all know, Mr. Speaker, that in order to try to develop, stimulate and promote any pride in a group of people or in their culture we must have a preliminary step such as the educational-cultural concept contained within this plan, with the hope that it will provide greater opportunity for the individuals who take part in the educational system to absorb a larger measure of knowledge than otherwise might be the case, and to have a greater degree of self-respect.
The government response to this plan was one of relative silence except the general cliche retort that the matter was "under study" and that in due course, or whenever a conclusion was reached, a public announcement would be made. I understand that on the 29th day of July this year the cabinet made a generally favourable determination with regard to educational-cultural institutions and programs for Indian people operated by and for themselves and for their own advancement. Apropos of that decision they concluded that since the Indian Association of Alberta, in March, 1970, was the first to present a proposal for a cultural-educational centre the pilot stage of that proposal should be the first to be considered for approval by a particular standing subcommittee of the cabinet.
The concept within that cabinet decision was that in the fiscal year 1971-72 $2 million would be available. We are now two-thirds of the way through that fiscal year. Some supplementary estimates were tabled a few days ago, and one would assume that, if the government intended to put money behind the concept, behind its decision, some provision would have been contained in those estimates for the first stage of the proposal by the Indian Association of Alberta. I have not been able to find any such amount in looking through the supplementary estimates. We all realize the supplementary estimates are phrased in such a way that it is often difficult to extract full knowledge of what is contained therein, but as I can read the proposals in those estimates there is nothing pertaining to this matter.
The cabinet decision of July also determined that $10 million would be available over the next five years funded equally between the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development and the Department of the Secretary of State. Involved in that decision was the necessity of a decision on the mechanics necessary to implement the plan. In other words, to carry forward into actual

accomplishment the decision that the cabinet made on July 29 a decision had to be made on the putting into effect and administration of the plan, not for the purpose of denying what cabinet had decided but for putting into effect what cabinet had decided, by the interdepartmental committee on Indian and Eskimo policy.
I should like to direct the House to yesterday's Hansard where this question was dealt with in what I think was a rather shallow approach on the part of the government and the minister in particular. As found on page 9802 of Hansard the Leader of the Opposition asked this question:
I specifically ask why a meeting of the interdepartmental committee on Indian and Eskimo affairs-
I assume he was talking about the interdepartmental committee on Indian and Eskimo policy which would presumably be one and the same thing.
-called to consider the recommendation of the standing subcommittee on the Alberta proposal, was cancelled?
The minister replied as follows, and perhaps for fear of being accused of only presenting that part which supports a particular position, I should read it all.
Mr. Speaker, I do not sit on that committee, so I do not know if the sittings have been cancelled. I can tell the hon. member that we have been discussing this subject for months with the officials of the Department of the Secretary of State and with the representatives of various Indian organizations in Canada but no conclusion has been reached yet.
I think it is well known that the minister does not sit on interdepartmental committees. These committees normally operate within the Public Service structure. I point out to the House and the minister the simple fact that the chairman of that interdepartmental committee on Indian and Eskimo affairs is the minister's own deputy minister, Mr. Robinson. He is the chairman of that interdepartmental committee on Indian and Eskimo affairs. Yet the minister had the effrontery to stand up in the House yesterday and say what he did. Technically, in replying to the question, he told the truth. But how does he know if what he said is right? He does not sit on the committee. What is going on, Mr. Speaker? Does the deputy minister operate in a vacuum? Does the minister now know what his deputy is doing in attempting to put into effect government policy?
The cabinet made a decision on July 29 and said, "Yes, we endorse the concept of educational-cultural centres for Indian people; yes, we think the Indian Association of Alberta's first stage of such a proposal should be endorsed and accepted; yes, we think we should put up $2 million in 1971-72 and $10 million in certain subsequent years." I would think that a minister who is at all concerned about what goes on in his department would know what his deputy minister is doing, especially if that deputy is the chairman of an interdepartmental committee that is supposed to put into effect a government program. Perhaps the minister is ignorant of what is happening in his department. Perhaps he is not all that concerned about what goes on. Perhaps somebody in his department is trying to subvert the decision of cabinet and deny to these people the opportunities that would be available to them as a result of the cabinet decision.
November 24, 1971

I think the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development has indulged in a sort of specious covering-up. He should not have done that. He is a nice gentleman, a kind gentleman, a decent sort of chap, Mr. Speaker, and really he should have known better. He should have told us what the interdepartmental committee was doing and what the deputy minister was doing with respect to cabinet policy in that area. Were they putting it into effect or were they denying cabinet the right to put that proposal into effect?
One could make allowances for what happened if this were a relatively minor, insignificant matter, but it is not. It involves a very fundamental and important question, namely, the educational opportunities of a few hundred thousand people in this country, the educational opportunities for a whole growing generation of Indian people. Education is the fundamental base which must be provided before the Indian people can fully advance, make progress and develop some self-respect. It is only in this way that they can be given the chance to make a go of it by themselves and for themselves.
In view of the importance of the subject, surely the minister ought to have some knowledge as to what the deputy minister is or is not doing in this area. He should know, especially, if the deputy minister is operating in such a way as to obstruct government policy or put obstacles in the way of its implementation. It is either that, or the minister is somewhat dumb about what is happening within his department.
There has been deliberate delay, Mr. Speaker. Perhaps there is some real reason why cabinet can make a decision on July 29, set out within the cabinet minute relating to that decision the full details regarding funding, the concepts and extension of this program over a four or five year period, and then delay the implementation of that program. Having spent years considering the matter, having spent months, as the minister said, in talking about it with the Secretary of State and with the Indian people, and having got to the point of making a decision to put the plan into effect, perhaps there is some reason why they do not want to do so at this time.
Knowing the way this government operates, and the precision of mind it has about events that are likely to happen next year, I am inclined to think they are more concerned about the impact such a program will have upon the Indian people at election time than now. Is that what this is? Election bait? It would not surprise me one bit. For the minister to operate in that way would be quite in keeping with the activities of a number of his colleagues who are more concerned about politics and political support than they are about benefits to the general public. I cannot see any other reason for it except incompetence, and the minister is not incompetent. We all know that. That sort of reasoning is a pretty big insult to the intelligence of the native Indian people. How can you expect them to fall for that?
I do not want to get too far into the area dealt with by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). I am referring to cabinet documents and the disclosure of what they contain or the leakage of them to the general public. I would not do this at all except Your Honour said this might more appropriately be a subject matter for debate than a question of privilege. There is

something revealing in the attitude of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) who we know is the head of the government. I will not read the quotation again. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre did that when he raised the question of privilege. It is true that the comment was made with regard to a query relating to the Gray report and not about this cabinet document of July 29, although they both fall in the same class. In other words, they are so-called confidential documents or documents which the government classed as confidential but which subsequently became public.
The remarks of the Prime Minister, which possibly are reflected in a decision of the government to put off dealing with this very important educational-cultural project, were both offensive and derogatory to a great many people in the Public Service. They indicate that the Prime Minister is very ambidextrous. He is able to use the tar brush and the whitewash brush with equal dexterity.

There is another question
involved here. It is a fundamental one, aside from the aspect I have raised. It is the question of treaty rights. Let those howling jackals in the background remember that this is fundamental before they start crying about responsibilities. The Indians in these three bands looked at the treaties which we signed and concluded that there is contained in them a responsibility to build schools on the reserves and to pay for the services of teachers. They are not talking about the type of schools which might have been built in the days when those treaties were signed. They are talking about modern-day schools. That is what the committee report talked about too, Mr. Speaker. It talked about a modern educational system, about the responsibility of the federal government, and said this matter should remain the responsibility of the federal government. Moreover, the committee recommended unanimously that the government should cease and desist from its attempts to slough off these educational responsibilities on the provinces.
This is why the people belonging to these bands decided to take their children out of school. It was in an effort to get a fair shake. The minister has classified their action as blackmail. He said he was being blackmailed and that as a consequence he did not intend to do anything further. Mr. Speaker, since when has it been blackmail to ask someone to live up to his honour, to respect treaties which are in existence, to carry out his responsibilities and discharge the high duties of ministerial office in an effective manner? But the minister howled "blackmail" and shut his door and stayed in Ottawa while saying on the floor of the House, as I gather he said elsewhere: "My door is open any time". I mentioned this to one of the members of the Indian Association of Alberta yesterday and he said:

"You bet the minister's door is open. And it opens from the inside."
The minister did not care enough about his responsibilities to go to the communities involved and see the situation at first hand or to talk to the Indians concerned and find out what was happening and whether he could do something directly. The cry of blackmail is simply the refuge of a person found delinquent in his duties. Oh, they had a meeting. They had a meeting in Winnipeg on mutual ground. I understand it was promoted by people who were neither in the government nor in the Indian Association of Alberta nor in any of the three bands involved in an attempt to find some area of neutrality within which an attempt could be made to resolve the problem. I understand that the minister attended but that he did not engage in any meaningful conversation with the people there. Rather, he repeated the declaration he had made earlier: You send the children back to school and I will then come and attend to you; when you alter the manner in which you are presenting your legitimate demands and let me carry out my duties and responsibilities, then I will come.
Certain allegations were made in the House yesterday. Whether those allegations had been made or not, whether or not there is any connection between the decision of the parents in those three bands to keep their children out of school in an attempt to force the minister to meet his obligations and the decision taken by the government not to put into effect the first stage of the Indian educational centre complex to which it had agreed on July 29-

speechtext:
The first part of your remarks, Mr. Speaker, was quite correct and I withdraw my reference to its being deliberate. It has been drawn to my attention that I have only a few minutes left, so I will not bother reading the telegram. I was interrupted many times in my attempt to read it. Let me simply say that the response that the principal secretary, or whatever he is called, to the Prime Minister gave to the president of the Indian Association of Alberta was both offensive to and derogatory of the president of the association and contributed to the gulf of misunderstanding, which is a point I also made yesterday.
Let me refer to what the report of the committee is attempting to do, what it is trying to correct, and to put this in general, historic perspective. Indian children have for many years gone through an educational program in which they have been treated to a second or even third-class education since the qualifications of their teachers were of much lower standard than those of the teachers available to the province. Any teacher who could not fit into the provincial scheme by reason of not being qualified, however incompetent they might be as teachers, could always find a haven in the education branch of Indian affairs. That was the situation some years ago.
In many respects the Indian people were punished for using their own language in certain schools that were operated by the federal government. They were given the feeling that as a group of individuals they were inferior. Their needs now probably require a much greater degree of education than the needs of the rest of society in order to counterbalance this inferiority feeling and to assist them to develop self-respect. We must try to establish for them a pride in their inheritance and reverse the damage done by teaching them trades and skills and by giving them the qualifications necessary to take their part in the economic activities of this nation.
The report of the committee also recognized that we must try to depart from the so-called general, white, middle-class standards and values of teachers generally who teach in Indian schools, that we should try to attempt to teach Indian standards to Indian children rather than ignoring them. We should try to teach skills and trades that will reverse and correct a situation where the dropout rate among Indian school children is now four times the national average. We must try to correct a situation where 50 per cent, to use a general, rounded figure, of the adult Indian population is unemployed and unable to find work.
I do not want to go through the committee's report point by point, but it does have a number of very worth-while and valuable sections. One recommends that over a phased period of five years we start pre-school instruction to children in the three-year age group, recognizing the necessity for bending over backward to ensure that the younger children are fully prepared to enter the educational system proper. It also recommends that language instruction at the pre-school level and in the first and second years of primary school should be in their native tongue initially, with either English or French as the

secondary language, and that the curriculum in the federal program should include and emphasize more the question of Indian history, the question of Indian culture, its music, its art and its value system in order to instil the degree of pride which is necessary. Another section of the report relates directly to the decision of parents who keep their children out of school. It reads:
-the government must immediately and in full consultation and partnership with the Indian and Eskimo people of Canada develop a federal education system as free from the deficiencies afflicting our present program as is humanly possible, and to this end your committee recommends-
Then they make certain recommendations which are contained in the report. People in a free society-this is what Indian people are in theory-can advance and be free only if their institutions are free. They can develop self-respect only if they are shown self-respect; for example, if the educational system in which they work and learn promotes the concept of self-respect. The Indian people have been the group most disadvantaged and discriminated against in Canada's history. The government, with its preoccupation about other matters, refuses to recognize the cultural and aboriginal rights of the Indian people and attempts to fit everyone into a slide-rule school. As I have said, the minister is a decent guy-but why doesn't he try to do some decent things?

Mr. Speaker, it gives me a good deal of pleasure to rise in support of the motion of the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard). The report in question was studied by the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development. After the hearing of many witnesses it was unanimously agreed to by the committee. I am anxious to hear the comments of members on the other side of the House on this question.
I believe it is fair to say that in a few areas this government's notion of a just society is a shambles and a farce in respect of the native people of Canada. In its insensitivity and basic intention, the government has attempted to impose upon the native people policies which do not meet their real needs or their legitimate aspirations. This approach and lack of action has been confirmed by the failure of the government to engage in genuine consultation with representatives of the native people and to develop a substantive program to help overcome their many difficulties.
I think it is fair to say that 15 or 20 years ago it was thought that integration of Indian students with students in our urban or large centres was perhaps the answer and would produce a significant number of Indian graduates. I think 15 years ago the Indian people themselves thought this might be the solution to an educational program which previously had not been successful. However, after a trial period-and I believe 15 years is a reasonable period-of attempting to integrate Indian students with other students in our schools this program has proven to be a disaster. We need only consider the number of dropouts of Indian students. When we see a drop-out rate of 94 per cent this is in no way an indication of a successful educational system. I think we can also say with some degree of assurance that the present policy of the government in no way promises to relieve this problem.
November 24, 1971

Mr. Speaker, I have met hundreds of Indian people. I have been in their homes, in their community halls and other places. Some of the meetings were attended by 100, 200 or 300 people. On these occasions one could look around and ask oneself how many teachers, engineers, lawyers and doctors were in the group. One might ask oneself how many of these people got past grade 12 or even grade 5.
Then one must ask the reasons for this. The reasons are, obviously, that the solutions so far put forward have been an absolute failure from the point of view of graduating Indian students into the professions I have mentioned. Some people in the past have expressed their discrimination against Indians by suggesting that the fault lies with the Indians themselves. They suggest, also, that perhaps Indians do not have the intelligence, that maybe they do not have the desire or the ambition. I think this kind of answer is too easy and too slick and it is not true.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: You are right.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I think it has been shown by many research people that the intelligence of the average Indian is no different from that of the average person. Given the fact that their intelligence is the same, we must accept the fact that the Indian people are interested in sending their children to school in order that they may obtain the education necessary for them to enter the professions and trades in order to look after themselves and their families. Given that situation, we must come back to the question of why they are not getting through school.
The answer, obviously, is that there must be something wrong with the system to which they are exposed. What is wrong with the system? It could be that these people have never been meaningfully involved in the system of education. We might consider the fact, for example, that in some parts of the country the Indian people cannot sit on school boards. This means that they have no influence over the kind of teachers hired or the kind of curriculum to which students are exposed. In general they have nothing to say about the subject matters which might be of interest to students.
As a result, the Indian people over the past few years have said, "This is enough," since they have suffered this kind of injustice for 200 years or more. They say it is time they took things into their own hands. I think that is fair enough. They say to us that we have been running their educational system for 100, 200 or 300 years and it has been a complete failure in respect of Indian students graduating from school.
They also say they want a chance to do it their own way. They want to have a say in who the teachers are. They want to screen the teachers in order to see whether there is the kind of prejudice which would make them unsuitable for teaching their children. They want to know whether the teachers have an understanding of the Indian way of life, so that they may be effective in an Indian community. The Indian people want to have an influence on the kind of curriculum their children are exposed to. They want to ensure that there are none of the old prejudices against Indians such as we read of in textbooks which portray the Indian as a savage, lurking around in a loincloth with feathers on his head. This is still the kind of image that many of our books depict about the Indian
Indian Affairs
population. Just imagine your child, Mr. Speaker, seeing portrayed in his school this image of his father and grandfather. I think it is very easy to understand that it is a degrading experience for a child to have this kind of image wrongly and constantly portrayed.
We had some success a year ago in the area of giving Indian people a little more say in their educational system. The school at Blue Quills, northeastern Alberta, was turned over to Indian control on an experimental basis. An education council was set up by the Indian people which is the equivalent of the school board and has had complete control over this school for the past year. They are now in their second year of teaching and I think I can say with assurance, after talking to some of the teachers, to some students and to some members of the education council, that it shows great promise. Innovations brought in by the people who are directly involved have already, in such a short time, shown evidence of tremendous progress in the education of the students who are attending the school.

To get a little closer to what has been happening in the last two days with regard to blackmail, I say that if anybody has been guilty of blackmail it is the minister, because he has given his assurance to the Indian Association of Alberta of participation in certain projects such as the educational cultural centre which was constructed 40 miles west of Edmonton. This was approved by the cabinet. The Indian Association of Alberta spent approximately $160,000 in research and development for this project and then they waited for the rest of the funds. They hired academics, consultants, and so on, and when the time came to pay them there was no money to do so because the minister had changed his mind. He said that the government had not yet decided whether they were going to go ahead with this project.
I point out, Mr. Speaker, that the $160,000 spent on this project was money allocated by the department. So there seems to be a discrepancy there. In view of the telegram sent by the Prime Minister's secretary, to which the hon. member for Skeena referred, there is no doubt in my mind that what the minister was saying to the Indian people was, "If you want to get your money you had better send your children back to school". If that is not blackmail I do not know what is.
There were a couple of other programs for which money was not forthcoming as promised. I am referring to the sports program which was designed to develop athletes among the Indian population for competition in the Canada Games and even possibly in the Olympic Games. The funds for these programs were withheld. There was a joint program between the government and the Indian Association, namely, the community development program. Funds for that were withheld. I should like the minister to explain the reasons for withholding these funds.

speechtext:
To take the matter a little further, the Indian people were at all times willing to negotiate with the minister and to prove this point they appointed two mediators, one from Ontario and one from Manitoba. These mediators succeeded in arranging a meeting between the chiefs from northeastern Alberta and the minister. The meeting took place. The purpose of the meeting was to have a preliminary discussion on how the problems could be resolved. The chiefs came to the meeting keeping in mind that it was to be a preliminary discussion. What did the minister do? He went there with seven or eight of his advisers and made a settlement with one of the chiefs from the smallest reserve, the one with the smallest demands. By this method he managed to drive a wedge into the strike. He sent the children of one reserve back to school and on the heels of that action the strike quickly broke down.
I was glad to see the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey) sitting with the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien) a few minutes ago because the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern development referred to the strike as being blackmail. I hope that he

had a chance to consult with the Minister of Labour on his view that the strike was blackmail, because how does this strike differ from any other strike?
The minister said he would not talk to the Indian people because if he did, all the Indian people in the country would go on strike and make all sorts of demands. This is possible and it might be a good idea. What is wrong with a strike by the Indian people to achieve that which they feel is necessary for themselves and their families? I cannot see how that can be more wrong than a strike by the postal union, by the farmers union or by any other union. This is simply one of the methods used in our society to help achieve settlement in areas where one is not forthcoming by any other method. It is a democratic method and I support it wholeheartedly.
I want to make a few more references to the fifth report of the Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development. What does it actually say? It reads in part:
-that something was drastically and basically deficient in an education system or systems with a school drop-out rate of more than four times the national average serving a population of which 40 per cent to 50 per cent of the adult males were unemployed or underemployed-
In the last couple of months, Mr. Speaker, there has been a great fuss in this House about a national unemployment rate of 7 per cent. The Indian people have been living with an unemployment rate of 40 per cent to 50 per cent, and in some communities it is 90 per cent or 100 per cent. Nothing is being done by the minister to solve this problem. He simply says, "We are doing what we can and some day we will solve it." That is not good enough.
Over the past three years the government verbally has indicated some good intentions. Members of the government told the Indian people that they wanted to talk to them, that they wanted the Indian people to tell them what they desired in order that the government could develop appropriate policies. Consultations were held with the Indian people and the government brought out a white paper-but it bore no resemblance to what the Indian people had requested during the consultative meetings.

It also said:
In those schools remaining under the control of the education branch-
Which is in the vicinity of 35 per cent of the schools.
-the committee believes that the objectives of the federal schools should be the creation of models of excellence which will furnish to Indian and Eskimo young people an education which will provide to them equality of opportunity and the ability to be employed at every level of the economy of the regions in which they live.
Just to touch on some other points, I think it is fair to say that the crux of the whole report is contained in the following phrase:
That the government should continue its policy-
I do not believe it is the policy at the present time: unfortunately, this wording is not exactly right.
-that no transfers of education programs from the federal level of provincial systems take place without the express and clear approval of the majority of the parents in each community concerned.
I must take issue with the report in this respect because it says that the government should continue its policy that no transfers be made. This is not the government's policy. If it were, there would be no strike in northeastern Alberta. I remind the hon. member for Rocky Mountain (Mr. Sulatycky) that the strike there is because the Indian people refuse to have their children transferred to schools situated in larger towns off the reserves. The strike started because the government would not co-operate with the Indian people in achieving their desire to have the schools on the reserves improved and updated. So, Mr. Speaker, this is an inaccuracy in the report. The report also makes reference to cultural and language instruction. It recommends:
That all curriculums within the federal program be revised to include:
(a)	Substantially more Indian history including Indian contributions to the economy, science, medicine, agriculture, exploration, etc.,
(b)	Special courses in Indian culture, music, art, handicrafts, etc. and that pressure be brought upon the respective provincial systems to inaugurate similar reforms wherever Indian children are being taught.
The report recommends that language instruction policies should be reviewed. It says:
That the language of instruction at the pre-school level and up to the first or second year of primary school should be in the language of the local Indian or Eskimo community with secondary and tertiary languages English and/or French being introduced gradually through the pre-school and primary period and that courses linked to the local Indian or Eskimo culture continue to be taught in the local language throughout the primary level of school.
This is a very important matter because in many cases Indian communities are isolated; the children have not been taught either English or French. When they go to school their entire day is spent in learning English or French and as a result they lose a year or two because the first couple of years are taken up in their attempts to pick up the language of instruction. The children become discouraged because listening to a language they do not understand does not stimulate their interest sufficiently to
Indian Affairs
create the proper motivation for them to stay in school as long as they should. I would refer hon. members who wish to know about the rest of the recommendations of the committee, to Votes and Proceedings of June 30, 1971.
I want to conclude by saying that because of poor planning, insensitive programming and severely limited opportunities, the standard of education available to most of the native peoples of Canada is abominable. Ninety-four per cent of the Indian and Eskimo children drop out of school before they reach grade 12, and the federal government is apparently attempting to phase out its program of support for Indian and Eskimo students who reach university. This is a disgraceful situation. It is in large part the result of the imposition on the native peoples of an educational system which is foreign to their culture and which does little more than cultivate alienation, frustration and resentment.
I would strongly recommend the establishment of a special task force, under the direction of qualified native people, which would develop teaching programs, curricula, text books and teaching aids which are relevant to the needs of and sensitive to the way of life of the native peoples. I would also support the establishment, wherever appropriate, of school boards composed entirely, or in large part, of the native peoples themselves with the power to hire teachers, design curricula and make similar decisions. Such school boards for the first time would involve the native peoples in their own educational programs and would greatly contribute to making their education more relevant and attractive to them.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I wish to make one or two comments about the minister, who seems to be losing interest in my remarks. I feel that he is not responding to the needs of the native peoples. He will not talk to the people whose affairs he is supposed to administer. It would be an understatement to say he has lost credibility with the native people. Therefore, I think he should be replaced. I think that the minister should be replaced by the minister responsible for housing. I have spoken to Indian people and they tell me they have had dealings with that minister, that he is a minister they can trust and that he understands their problems with more sympathy than the present minister. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I recommend that to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) before he loses more credibility than he is at present.
In conclusion, government policy which seeks to achieve a healthy, productive and economically secure life for the native people of Canada must respect their cultural heritage and aspirations. The Canadian Indian must be free to choose to live in or away from his native community without prejudicing the opportunities available to him to enjoy the standard of living and quality of life of other Canadians. In the formulation and operation of such policy our native people must be fully consulted and involved. The obligations of history must be met in a new approach to the problems of the native people of Canada, an approach which is sensitive, fair, constructive and is developed in active partnership with them.

Mr. Speaker, for the past one and a half hour, we have been hearing discussions on Indian affairs in Canada.
I have been listening carefully to the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) who has raised the matter of the report of the Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development, as well as to the hon. member who has just resumed his seat.
I sincerely believe that the Indian problem is one of the most serious. I would even say that it is too serious to be made the subject of a political game in this House, and that we should not use the Indians as a political balloon. It is nice to say, for the record and for newspapers, how much we are concerned with Indians and Eskimos, but we should still keep a certain sense of honesty.
Last year I had the opportunity of going to Yellowknife where some Indians met the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien). I am not here to commend or flatter the minister when there is no reason for it. But last year when I went there, I noticed that the minister was seriously looking into problems met by Indians in northern Alberta and elsewhere in Canada. And I must say it publicly.
In the House reference is made to Indians in order to prove that the government has done nothing for them. Some members even attack the government, blaming federal officials and claiming that only one political party is on their side, etc.
Mr. Speaker, we have had enough of this political clowning. Indians deserve much better treatment than what they are getting nowadays in the House of Commons.
Last week while in Edmonton I was invited to appear on the Dave Ward show. Mr. Dave Ward, coming from an Eskimo family, discussed the Indian-Eskimo issue in Canada. These people are not asking us for our culture but rather want us to help them keep their own. They ask us permission to be themselves.
People say that Indians do not go to university, do not become lawyers, doctors or chartered accountants. However, those who want to become lawyers or go to university can do so. They are not forced to do it. It would not be a good thing to make it compulsory.
Eskimos and Indians in my area travel from the northern reaches of Hudson Bay by plane at the government's expense, to study in Rouyn-Noranda. They have no obligation but they are told: If you want, come. Those who are willing to study can do so. As for those who do not wish to study, let us help them remain where they are and keep on fishing and hunting.
I was listening recently to a program televised from Winnipeg during which I heard an Indian from northern Manitoba who was working in a plant in Winnipeg say that he was not interested in working there. He wanted to be able to live at home, in the woods and close to a lake, fishing and hunting because he has been brought up this way, this is his culture, what he has been trained for.
I understand that thousands of dollars are granted every year to Indians to help them live in suitable dwellings in northern Canada. There are certainly shortcom-

ings. Nothing is perfect. If the progressive Conservatives are so kind to Indians, why did they not settle the Indian problem when they were in power?
When the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) who is sitting over there, was Prime Minister, people wearing feathers on their head sat in the galleries to protest against the government not taking action in the area of Indian affairs. Nothing could be done at the time but today they want to blame the whole thing on the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development saying that he is inefficient and should be replaced by the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Andras), or by the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Davis). While we are about it we could replace him by just any one at all. It would not improve matters one whit.
Let us at least be objective. Let us make suggestions. We are dealing with education. There is an education problem. Are any of our teachers, whether from Ontario, Alberta, prepared to go and teach in the north of Manitoba or Quebec or wherever? It is a problem of teachers.
I think that instead of interfering to such a degree in the field of Indian education, the government should have left that to the Protestant and Catholic missionaries who looked after almost all Indians a few years ago and gave a better education than any government could give. Moreover, the missionaries were on the spot the year round. But they were left out. It would have cost much less to the government to help those missionaries-either Catholic or Protestant-who were ready to serve all Indian and Eskimo families. But we discouraged them, forced them to leave and replaced them by bureaucrats whose work is unsatisfactory most of the time because of their inefficiency.
I should like to repeat what Mr. Dave Ward said last week in Edmonton: "We do not ask you to give us your white culture. We do not want to become white people; we want to stay as we are. We do not want anything to be forced upon us. We want to be free; that is all we ask."
But in the House of Commons, for God's sake let us stop fooling with the Indian or Esquimo people and using them as a political stepping-stone to serve the political interests of some people. When a member rises in the House to say he is the only protector of Indian and Esquimo people, the only one to know the Esquimo problems, I feel disgusted. Truth still has its rights as well as honesty.
It is a good thing to make suggestions to the hon. minister. Should the hon. minister blunder, let us tell him. But let us not use the Indians in order to say: Listen, the Progressive Conservatives are better than you Liberals. The New Democratic Party members are superior because most of them are Indians.
The Indians can be used to serve one's petty political interest. In my opinion, the debate should be upgraded and not downgraded. We should offer logical suggestions. I repeat that I think the most logical suggestion was made last week by Mr. Dave Ward when he said that we should enable Indians who want it to further their education and those willing to remain as they are to keep on being hunters, fishermen, trappers and craftsmen. We should
November 24, 1971

help them be themselves and not force them to be like us. This is what they want.
I therefore invite the hon. minister to consider not only the economic aspect, but also the social and cultural aspects of the Indian and the Eskimo situation, so that they feel more at home in Canada since, after all, they are similar to us and are living in the same country. Let us treat them as they want to be treated and let us stop blindly blaming those people who at least have the decency of doing their utmost to improve the plight not only of the Indians and the Eskimos but of the whole Canadian population.
