speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, of course not all the kids were back to school. Yet 92 per cent of the kids at Saddle Lake are back at school, and all the Keeheewin kids are back at school. The kids at Cold Lake are not back in school. That means that 1,000 out of 1,275 are back. From the beginning I wanted to settle the strike and I want to tell the House today that the kids were on strike before I received any news or any demands by the Indians. I myself sent, in September, with the agreement of the Indian Association of Alberta, a representative there. He was supposed to be there in good faith. That is how it was accepted in my office by the parties. This representative, one of my assistants, went there to visit the northern reserve. When he arrived in Edmonton the same people who had agreed to have him go there and investigate facts had a demonstration against him at the airport. This is purely and simply politics of the worst type. This man had gone in good faith. He went to the reserve and when he came back he made a report to me. Within three hours of getting that report I gave orders to do what had to be done at that moment.
I said to the people of the Keeheewin reserve, "It is true; you need a new kindergarten and you will get it." Three hours after I received the report I said that. I sent them a telegram and told them that they will have up to grade 3 schooling on the reserve. That is what I decided three hours after I received the report. But the same people from the Indian Association of Alberta told them not to accept what we were doing because it was purely piecemeal. When I met the chief of the Keeheewin, Chief Gordon Young Chief, a good chief, he asked of me, at the meeting in Winnipeg that hon. members referred to,

November 24, 1971
Indian Affairs
exactly what I had offered him on October 5. However, people were using the chief to play politics, and that is why I shall go before the committee tomorrow and give all the facts. We should nt play politics with this problem. It is too important a problem.
I have visited Indians in all the provinces and in all the different parts of Canada. I have visited all the Eskimo and Indian settlements in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon never before visited by a minister.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Surely that is not correct.

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: I sat with the Indians for hours and hours and listened to them. But the problem is very difficult; the problem of education is the most difficult problem. It is the government that has asked the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development to look into the question of education. They prepared a report which we received on June 30. An order of the House was given to the committee to look into this matter. We received the report a few months ago. We are studying it. There are many good things in the report. The members of the committee have done a hell of a good job. They did not act in a partisan way. I congratulate them for the good work they have done.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: I have said many times, as the hon. member for Temiscamingue (Mr. Caouette) said, that what the Indians want is to be socially and economically equal in Canada and culturally different. The government is not shy when it comes to admitting that it is trying to find more money for cultural centres for the Indians. We want to do something. However, we cannot spend millions of dollars without developing some criteria and rules for the administration of those moneys.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Most of the Indian associations in Canada are very responsible. They are doing a good job. They try to do something good for their people. However, rather than negotiate with me in my office or elsewhere, some prefer to state their case over television. If they want to do it that way, that is their problem. However, that is not the way to do it. They say they are unable to meet the minister. They say they appeared over television because they did not receive a phone call to attend a meeting. They say they were not involved in the strike.
I stopped in Winnipeg. I am not shy. I said I would not meet the chiefs of the reserves because in conscience I was not satisfied that the purpose was to solve the problem. They only wanted to use these poor Indians of northern Alberta to serve their own purposes.
I hope that members will not only question me in committee tomorrow but will question the operations on the other side of the coin. I think some people are trying to develop some sort of bureaucracy of their own.
I talked to the chief of the Keeheewin reserve. I told him that I recognized there were many problems on his reserve. I asked him to tell me how many times the community development officers, who are paid by the Indian

Association of Alberta, visited his reserve to help him. He replied that they had never been there. We have negotiated these agreements with the Indians in that province in order to give them an opportunity to run some programs. This was not to help them sit around in offices in Edmonton dreaming up strikes but to go into the field and do the work for their people.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
This is the point that must be clarified. There are people who play politics and try to leak documents. I have nothing to hide. I said that yesterday. I volunteered to appear before the committee to explain the policies because I want this House to understand that this is the most difficult social problem that we have in Canada. We should not play politics with it. I am willing to open all the books.
Some people complain because committee meetings have been cancelled. I agree that one committee meeting was cancelled but another subcommittee was working during that time. The work was proceeding. Some people play politics, but we have not stopped working. I am responsible to all the Indians of Canada and all the Indian associations of Canada. I will not give premium to irresponsibility. I will not put grease on the squeaking wheel. In carrying out my duty I hope to treat all the Indian associations of Canada on the same basis.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Over the years we have done a lot to try to solve the problems of the Canadian Indians. We have tried to solve some of the problems. What makes me angry is that a member such as the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Yewchuk) should stand in his place and accuse me of forcing the Indians to attend a provincial school in Alberta when I know that agreements were signed in 1961 when the hon. member's party was in power.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Not in British Columbia.

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: I am talking about Alberta. I will come to British Columbia later. When we introduced our policy in the House on June 25, 1969, all the members of the opposition said that it was a hell of a good policy. Speaking for his party, the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) said there was only one thing wrong with it; it was 25 years too late.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: That is not true.

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Take the heat a bit.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: You know that what you are saying is not true. Check the record. Tell the truth.

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
We are trying to solve the problem but it is difficult. Less than three weeks ago I was in New Brunswick. I met with two different bands. One chief wanted his own school on his very small reserve. The other band wanted to go into an integrated system. I looked into the problem of the band that wanted its own school. The chief was not satisfied because the provincial government was not doing a fair job but that can be corrected. I think the
November 24, 1971

fact that the children in northern Alberta are attending a provincial school is not the problem. It is because they are not welcome in the provincial school. The hon. member for Athabasca should speak to his own provincial government to get them to do something about this.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: I have tried to keep the debate above politics. I will keep it that way.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: It is good that you have a little humour in your speech.

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I want to state the facts. Some people try to create the impression over the CBC that they will not accept any more money. I know these same people were in the offices of other ministers trying to get some money not later than yesterday. They would like to have money for which they will not be accountable. As a minister of the Crown I cannot accept that concept. We should sign agreements with the Indians but they should be treated like other people. They should provide us with the accounts we require after they have received the money.
I am unhappy because many of these problems have built up over a long period of time. I kept quiet about them. However, people living in glass houses should not throw stones. I think it was a shame that those who appeared on the program last Sunday tried to create the impression that they would not accept money from us. They were referring to money for which they are accountable, not money for which they are not accountable.
I think that when we are contracting with any organization in the land we should apply the same financial rules as to all other organizations. One of my fears is that in a controversy of this sort, when some are playing too much politics, it may harm a lot of other Indian associations in Canada who are doing a damned good job, associations which try to accelerate improvements in their educational facilities through consultation with the provinces and the federal government. I hope that because some people are trying to play politics with this subject we shall not harm the work of those engaged in these organizations, people who have acted very responsibly. What I see at the moment is this: there are some who are finding a new way of building their own little empires without taking into account the best interests of their own people.
When it is said that I used these Indian centres as a carrot on a stick in the Alberta situation, I disagree. Let me tell the House the facts. They said they had that document in their possession in September. In September there were only 250 children, more or less, on strike. The bulk of them were on strike in October. The Saddle Lake people, 1,000 of them, went on strike on or about October 15. So probably a month earlier they had this document which was alleged to have been leaked to them. The strike took place after they had this document, according to their own story. It is a pure lie that we tried to use these centres as a carrot on a stick.
I had occasion to meet with the association at the end of September when we discussed the situation in Alberta. Nobody talked to me at that time about the cultural cen-
Indian Affairs
tres situation. Nobody from there since that time has talked to me about it. I heard that from the Indian Association of Alberta over television. When I met them in Winnipeg they did not raise that question.
It is said I went there to impose my own solution. That is not the case. I listened to them, and what Chief Gordon Young Chief asked me at that meeting was exactly what I had offered him on October 5. But there were some who for political purposes told him not to accept it at that time. That is a shame, because the children have lost one month of schooling.
I have said I will never accept the practice of putting pressure upon the government by using their children in an effort to achieve their goal. Everyone in the House should support that position.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: If you let that happen one never knows what will be the result. I well know that Indian children in our society are sufficiently handicapped as things are at present and that they should not lose even one day of schooling. Even though we may think our behaviour is very good I know well that the Indian children are often not welcomed in our society. Rather than play politics with this subject the hon. member for Athabasca should talk to the people of his province to make them aware of the problem and make sure that the children are all welcome in the schools and elsewhere.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Members opposite thrust out great ideas. The hon. member for Athabasca said we should set up Indian school boards. Mr. Speaker, I have already started that process even in his own area; the Blue Quill School is administered by the Indians, and it is the first time in the history of Canada that such a thing has happened. Now I am working on a similar program in northern Saskatchewan.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: It was after another strike.

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: That is the kind of mistake the Indians made too. I did not agree because of the strike but because the proposal was a good one. I was not impressed for a minute by the strike. I looked at the suggested solution and I accepted it because it was a good solution, not because of the strike.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: But some of the Indians thought the strike was a good tool and they tried it this year once again. But this time the solution was not the right one. I do not think we should keep the Indians on the reserves and not permit them at an earlier age to be with the other students of Canada. I do not want to force the Indians to stay on the reserves as was the old policy. I want to open Canada to them. I want them to have the advantage of attending the best schools available in the area in which they are living, whether federal or provincial. I am working on a scheme right now under which the white people adjacent to a reserve in one part of Canada will go to school on the reserve-a reversal of previous integration.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Hear, hear!

November 24, 1971
Indian Affairs

Mr. Speaker I think we have done much up to date. I could venture to give figures establishing that we have more than doubled our expenditures with regard to Indians. We went from zero to $1 million to help the Indian Association of Alberta but I do not think this would really bring anything to this debate.
I think the House has lost precious time because we accepted yesterday to appear before the Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development tomorrow morning at eleven o'clock. As I said, I have absolutely nothing to hide. We must continue to work and try to improve the condition of the Indians and I hope we will do it in a non partisan way.
We hope that the progress already made will not slow down our efforts. No doubt there exist problems with the education of the Indian population, but as the hon. member for Temiscamingue said a while ago some of them are not ready to accept our education system. Some of them are not too interested in becoming university graduates. We must however continue to try and give to those who want it the possibility of becoming university graduates.

We should look at this problem in perspective. Do not forget that 12 or 13 years ago only 15 per cent of the Indian children were going past grade five. Now they all go beyond grade five. The drop-out problem is in grade 12. Of course it is a bad situation, but we have made a hell of a lot of progress. Thirteen years ago there were virtually no Indians attending universities. This year there are 800 Indians in universities.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
When we compare this figure with the 400 who attended universities last year, we find the number has doubled in one year.
There is much more I could say along the same lines but I do not feel it would be helpful to do so now. I appeal to Members of Parliament not to play politics with this issue. I am very happy to be Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. It is a tough job. I realize that the Indians had seven ministers in seven years before I became minister. At least I have offered a certain continuity in thinking. But I am not the kind of man who will allow himself to get cornered and who will bow under pressure. It is too bad, but I am not a yes-man. I look at proposals which are made and if they make sense I will approve them. But if they make no sense I shall say no.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I have heard people say there is a lack of communication with the Indians. Mr. Speaker, never has there been so much consultation with the Indians as in the last four years. I have attended annual meetings of Indian associations across the land. Sometimes I could not accept because of other commitments-as it happened, one such occasion arose last fall. But we are willing to listen. We are willing to discuss. At some point, though, I think the Indians will have to come up with some solutions and propositions. For example, when the Indian Association of Alberta came here in June, 1970 with their red paper

and they made the suggestion that there should be a joint committee of ministers and Indians to discuss all these problems, I agreed. Then they said no, they were not interested any more. So what the hell could I do in a situation like that?

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I do not think I have been arrogant. I think I am pretty well down to earth and do not fly in the sky too much. But we have to ask people to be reasonable, to make some propositions to us instead of just asking us to give them all the money. If we were sure that the money would be spent well, that would be fine. But what is going to happen if we create a monster as far as the Indians at the reserve level and the administration are concerned? What is going to happen if we have no control? I am not responsible to some of these self-appointed leaders; I am responsible to the Indians at the band level.
I want to decentralize by giving more authority to the bands. Many housing and welfare programs are administered at the band level by Indians in the band, and this does help solve their problems. But we should not be boxed into a situation where we create a bureaucracy between the Indians at the band level and the federal government. We need the Indian associations very badly so we will know what the problems are, and the provincial governments need them too. There should be these pressure groups, not establishments of the kind that they complain we have here. This is why my aim is to decentralize at the band level, because in this way more responsibility is given to the Indians to solve their problems.
I suggest we should not become too excited about those who try to make political mileage out of the situation, who try to create for themselves a good image on television. It is very seldom that the media in Canada report any progress on Indian problems, which does an injustice to the Indians themselves because on many reserves in Canada much progress has been made. Housing programs have been implemented in British Columbia and in Alberta on the Blood Reserve where a prefabricated housing project is under way. In Quebec at Loretteville not one Indian is on welfare. Other Indian reserves are making similar progress. But no mention is made of this; all we hear about is what remains to be done.
I recognize that we have a long way to go, but nevertheless we have made progress. I think this progress has been made by the government and by the House without partisanship so far, and it is too bad that some people have decided to be partisan at this particular moment.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives me a great deal of pleasure to rise at this point in the debate in support of the motion of the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) that the fifth report of the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development presented to the House on June 30, 1971 be concurred in.
I have a number of reasons for wanting to speak on this occasion. First of all, may I say we have listened to quite a lecture from the minister-

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
A diatribe.
November 24, 1971

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
A diatribe, it is suggested-about people not getting political over problems confronting our Indian people. I do not think that any member of this House has deliberately tried to get political on this matter, but the minister for one should not take that attitude. Neither do I intend to enter into the situation surrounding the school strike in northern Alberta nor to comment on the minister's assertion that he felt he was more responsible to the Indian Association of Alberta than to the people of this particular tribe.
My feeling is that when this strike took place and the minister was invited to meet the people on the reserve, the parents of the school children affected, he had every obligation to do so. The minister said that he felt otherwise, that he had no obligation or responsibility to meet that request. He went on to say he should not meet these people until the strike had been settled. I fully realize that the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien) is not responsible for the actions of his colleagues in cabinet, but it is a little difficult to understand why he feels he should not put in an appearance before a group of people who feel aggrieved until they settle their differences themselves.
As far as the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey) is concerned, there have been many instances of strikes being called and he has decided not to take any action. Similarly, there have been instances where it appears the minister felt that a solution to the strike could be assisted by his appearance, and thus he has taken part in the issue.
How many times have we seen delegations come to Ottawa, line up in their hundreds in front of the Parliament Buildings, and when the television cameras and microphones are ready minister after minister basks in the glory of television coverage as he addresses the assembly? I do not think the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development should attempt to tell the House that he feels ministers should not take part in these confrontations unless the disputants settle their troubles themselves.
The minister went on to say that the government was quite willing to put up money for certain projects that benefit the Indian people but that the government was also concerned about accounting for the money. The government wanted to be sure that all accounts duly authorized were turned in to the government before any expenditure was approved. I would ask the minister and some of his colleagues on the front benches whether they saw fit to do this in some of the fiascos of the Opportunities for Youth program last summer. If a question should be placed on the order paper asking for accountability for all the money spent on the Opportunities for Youth Program, I wonder whether the government could come forward with justifiable vouchers for all those expenditures.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Sure it can.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Guay) says, "Sure it can". I would be very pleased to confer with him one of these days to see whether he can give me-I have been waiting for it for some time-information on that subject. The government has not yet been able to come up with an answer.
Indian Affairs
I am very interested in this motion. I am sure all members of this House who over the years have repeatedly spoken on behalf of our native people fully realize how difficult it is to obtain action in respect of representations which the Indian people of Canada make to their representatives.
The fifth report of the Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development deals entirely with the subject of Indian education. In this report we have, I believe, one of the first real breakthroughs to solving most of the problems confronting our native people. On many occasions I have spoken to groups in all the Indian communities in northern Manitoba. As I am sure other members who represent areas in which Indian people live will know, the first thing the elderly people bring to our attention is the necessity for a good education for their children. Immediately I say this I am sure some members who are not involved with these problems day in and day out will ask why, if these people are so interested in the education of their children, we have such a high drop-out rate. This is a good question and it should be answered.
One reason we have such a high drop-out rate is the absolute frustration of Indian children over the years in endeavouring to get an education. All of us know about the system which was in vogue for many years, that of residential schools whereby children were taken away from their parents for periods of up to nine months or more in the year. These children were completely disassociated from their families. I am sure we are all aware of the tremendous frustrations those children faced in being away from their families. Many of them were sent to school at the age of five or six. They left their homes for the first time and in many cases were not even able to understand the English language. In those years this system was not given very much consideration. In fact, as was mentioned earlier in this debate, on many occasions these children were chastised for speaking their own language.
The fifth report of the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development tries very seriously to deal with many of the problems which for years have confronted the Indian people. I shall not go over all the sections of the report. However, I feel it is my duty to point out very clearly to the House, although it has been mentioned before, that one of the important aspects of the report is that which relates to pre-school teaching and recommends that children have a year or two of instruction in their mother tongue, and when they grow older that they not only be allowed but be encouraged to continue in an educational program which deals with their own culture and background.
During his remarks the minister referred to the number of students of Indian origin who are now at university compared to the few who were in that category a number of year ago. He pointed out that this is a great improvement. It is an improvement, but it is not enough. Unfortunately I was called out of the House for the first minute or two of the minister's address and perhaps I missed something. However, I listened to practically all of his speech and heard no assurance that the government plans to implement any of these recommendations in the near future.

November 24, 1971
Indian Affairs

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: You could have said, "that they would support concurrence".

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
It has been mentioned that I should have said something about the government supporting concurrence. Mr. Speaker, I think it is a very good conclusion that they will support concurrence, with the minister's recommendation, because the minister said he is not difficult to deal with and is very sympathetic to the problems of the Indians and their suggestions. I hope he is just as sympathetic to the unanimous recommendation of the Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development.
A few days ago in the newspapers-these reports have emanated from the front benches and the back benches of the government side of the House-we read the suggestions put forward by the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Deachman) in an effort to project to the people of Canada just how the House of Commons could be made much more effective. His suggestions were based solely on the idea, which as I say has been voiced by many people supporting the government, that the House of Commons should be closed from time to time and that more and more work should be given to committees so that the time of the House of Commons would not be wasted in just listening to debate.

speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) says, "Hear, hear". I say to him, through you, Mr. Speaker, that if the government feels it cannot give concurrence to this unanimous report, then on what basis does it feel that more and more work should be passed on to the committees? For the last three years I have said that the committee system in this House is in many ways a farce. The people of Canada are told that we have committees. Many members, representing all parties of this House, put in many hours on committee work. They do a lot of research and attend many meetings. However, this is not the first occasion on which concurrence has not been given by the government to a committee report. In this instance, after doing all this work the committee comes up with a unanimous report to the government and the government refuses concurrence. Therefore I say the committee system of the House of Commons has fallen into very evil days.
I said that I was particularly interested in speaking at this time because the subject dealt with in the fifth report of the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development can be a real breakthrough for the Indian people. Education is the basis for solving their problems. Many of the items mentioned in this report, such as the establishment of day schools in reserves, doing away with residential schools, the establishment of pre-school instruction, allowing the children to be taught in their own language until a certain grade, and the continuation of a well thought-out program taking into account the history of these people and their culture, are so important that I cannot see any reason why the government should not only give concurrence to the report but act on it immediately.

I would like to refer to a copy of a letter which is addressed, I understand, to all or most of the Indian chiefs in Canada. I am not criticizing the letter; I am very pleased that it has been written. It is signed by the Chairman of the Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development, the hon. member for Laprairie (Mr. Watson). In one paragraph the chairman writes as follows:
Although the government is free, under parliamentary rules to accept or reject in whole or in part the committee's report, the fact that the report was unanimously approved by committee members from all political parties obliges the government to give it serious attention.
All he asks for in that letter is that the government give this report serious attention. But it is frustrating and disappointing to all members of the House to listen to what was in my opinion a fairly headstrong lecture by the minister, which took about 20 to 25 minutes, in which the minister failed to indicate to the House the intentions of the government with regard to the report.
The minister said that people should not get political over problems of our native peoples. I think it is good that on their behalf we can get political at times, because if it were not for a great number of people bringing this matter into the political arena I suggest that little or nothing would have been done in the past nine or ten years.
The minister also said that he does not feel he should go out and meet groups of Indian people who have a complaint, unless they can settle differences among themselves prior to his meeting with them. Not many years ago the government produced what was reported to be the government's policy on Indian people. Granted, they said that nothing in that policy would be introduced without full consultation with the Indian people, but they stated very firmly to anyone who cared to listen that those were their proposals and they would not change them. If the minister or anyone else wishes to dispute this with me I would refer, after what has happened in the last week or two when we have seen a number of leaks of government documents, to what was perhaps one of the first leaks of government information pertaining to our Indian people. It happened just months after the issuance of the government's policy regarding Indians.
I raised the matter in the House, as others did. At that time we were in possession of a copy of a contract which the Liberal government had entered into with an Indian person in Calgary. He was under contract with the government to assist the government in finding ways and means whereby the Indian people of Canada would accept the policies of the government. When we brought out these points in the House, at first it was indicated that there was no knowledge of this; but when the government was confronted with a copy of the contract which they entered into with this person, they admitted that this had been so. If memory serves me correctly, we endeavoured to find out how many other people had been under the same type of contract but were not successful in obtaining an answer.
When the minister stands before the House and says that he has nothing to hide, I am not arguing with that. But when he says he is willing to do whatever he can for the Indian people, and the government offers the guaran-
November 24, 1971

tee that they will not put the proposed policy for the Indian people into effect without full consultation with the Indian people while at the same time they hire undercover people to try to assist them in finding ways and means of convincing the Indian people to accept their programs, then I say that the government is certainly not being fair to our Indian people.
In conclusion I would like to say that the fifth report of the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development deals with a serious matter regarding our native people. Among other things concerning educational matters in the report there is mention of the requirements on television. Again I come back to the words of the minister who spoke before me in this debate and indicated that the government is willing to do whatever it can for the Indian people. The other day I raised this matter in the House. For two successive days I tried to put the question to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, and on both days he was in his seat. I was recognized on the third day but the minister was not in the House. Therefore I directed the question to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau).
I asked if the government had any plans to provide financial assistance for the provision of television service to Indian communities with large populations, such as Cross Lake and Norway House in northern Manitoba. I can easily understand that the Prime Minister could not be expected to give an answer offhand at that time and I recall that the suggestion was made that I raise the matter on the "late show." But the least I expected the Prime Minister to do was assure me that he would pass my question to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien). I received no such assurance from him. Now that the minister is here, I suggest that he and his cabinet colleagues should combine on many of these matters and try to understand the problems that face them.
I suppose we will have to wait to see if the government will concur in the adoption of this report, but while the minister is in the chamber I would like to point out to him that there are many centres in Canada where Indian people reside in large numbers, and that are not served by television. I am certain that if equal populations of nonIndian origin were living in those centres, some television service would be provided for them. I defy any member of this House to point out other areas of Canada with populations around the 10,000 mark which have no access to television. Although many people complain about the type and quality of television programming, the provision of television service for these centres would be of great benefit, particularly for Indian children.
I have nothing more to say at this time. Mr. Speaker, but I repeat that having listened to the minister's statement I think it is a foregone conclusion that the government will concur in the adoption of this report.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker as a member of the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development which unanimously approved this report, I can honestly say that it is an important document in terms of defining the limitations and
Indian Affairs
strengths of the educational program to be developed in the future for the Indian and Eskimo peoples.
I was taken aback by the approach of the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Yewchuk) who attempted to turn the tables on the minister by indicating that school strikes called by Indian parents in northeastern Alberta were somehow related to the problems that the Indian Association of Alberta has with the federal government concerning two particular grants. I do not intend to go into that particular matter but I would like to look back over the few years that I have been in Parliament and point out the dramatic change which has taken place in the education of native peoples north of the sixtieth parallel.
In 1965, when I first became associated with the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, statistics indicated that approximately only 25 per cent of the kids in the Territories were attending school. Today, virtually all children in the Territories have an opportunity to attend educational facilities right through from kindergarten to primary school, secondary school and, under the programs of the local governments and federal government, to attend university or post-secondary vocational institutions.
I acknowledge that governments started on these educational programs too late. I acknowledge that initially many mistakes were made. We still have a long way to go, but I would like to underline some of the improvements that have been made in the north. The first schools were of only one or two classrooms, located in small communities stretched across the Arctic and down the Mackenzie, and after the first few grades children were airlifted to larger communities where they lived for eight or nine months of the year in school hostels. This created a breakdown in the pattern of family life.
Many native families continued to trap and hunt and to live outside settlements for the greater part of the year. Now virtually every community in northern Canada has schools that educate up to grade 8, after which students are moved to the larger centres to attend high school. We have also seen the establishment of seasonal-type school hostels which permit parents to continue their traditional way of life, hunting, trapping and sealing, leaving their children in their home community to attend school without a break and returning to live with their families after the hunting season is over.
This committee report is a hardnosed document. All of us who served on the committee tried as best we could, within the limitation of our abilities, to identify the problems and suggest solutions. We know that in the past educational facilities were not adequate in the northern parts of some of the provinces. We know that in northern communities housing, sanitation systems and economic opportunities were lacking to a great degree. What we are honestly trying to find is some balance whereby the native peoples will be able to participate in the Canadian way of life, socially and economically, while still retaining their own culture.
In the last four years I have observed the actions of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien). Ever since the day he was appointed to that position he has tried to improve conditions for the native peoples. Three and a half years ago he started a

November 24, 1971
Indian Affairs
consultation program and either he or one of his colleagues visited Indian communities across Canada and told the people, "Tell us what you want so that we as a government will be able to put some ideas down on paper." We then saw the white paper. This was greeted almost unanimously by members of the House as being a major move forward.

Then we saw the reaction of the Indian people. Very quickly the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said to them, "Come and tell us what you want". The Indian Association of Alberta came to Ottawa and presented their red paper, a well thought-out, well worded and positive document. We have seen the funding of the various Indian-Eskimo associations so that they could take upon themselves some of the responsibilities formerly carried out by government. All that is well recognized. In this process of change there are bound to be problems and confrontations. This is part of the purpose of the funding program-so that the Indian people can finally tell the rest of the country what they want, what they have in mind and how they want to do it.
I can speak only of the various associations in the Northwest Territories, but at one site the only serious contact the Indian people had with the administration was through the local representative or at the treaty parties which took place once a year. These were very minimal situations that I personally have always been ashamed to participate in as a white person. This situation has changed. The Indian people are now putting forward their ideas. Sometimes they shock the white community, and maybe this is not a bad thing. Sometimes they come forward with ideas that government cannot accept because of lack of funds or other reasons. However, in other cases it is possible for the government to work out some form of agreement or arrangement whereby the desires and ambitions of the Indian people, through their associations, can be recognized and adjustments made.
In the educational process, Mr. Speaker, we see some rapid developments. I should like to mention what is happening in a native community called Rae which is 70 miles northwest of Yellowknife. For many years the Indian children of that community either went into the bush with their parents during the school year or were moved to hostels at Fort Smith or Fort Simpson where they were away from their parents for approximately ten months of the year. The government suggested that a new school should be built in the vicinity of the community. The site of the community itself was unsatisfactory because of its location. For three, four or five years negotiations took place between the chief of the band council, other members of the Indian community and the administration, not only to determine where the school should be located but what form it should take once it was agreed that it should be constructed.
A decision on location was reached very quickly by the Indian people. The area was named after one of the great chiefs of the Dogrib band and in order to ensure complete participation by the community, arrangements were made to establish an education committee. This committee visit-

ed a number of educational institutions in the United States and Canada. It brought in its own advisers who were funded by the government. It was agreed that a school designed on the open-school concept would be proceeded with and that the hostels would be of a design best suited to small groups of children; and, more important, that the administration of the curriculum would be the responsibility of the people of the community. Subsequently, the Edzo-Rae school board was established. The school is now in operation, teachers have been hired by the community, hostel supervisors and even the cooks for the kitchen have been hired.
This is the type of forward thinking that can take place and is taking place. As I said earlier, we know it is not going far enough, fast enough. But as Members of Parliament and representatives of our constituents we can continue to encourage the minister, the representatives of his department and provincial governments and show that there is a great need for participation. Participation is necessary so that the benefits will return to our Indian youngsters who have so much to offer to this country and to their own people.
Again, I should like to say publicly that I believe the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development has taken tremendous strides in the last 3 j years.

-any Indian person or any Indian group. He has gone out of his way to meet all the Indian people. I think the minister explained his side of the story in a way that the people of Canada will acknowledge. He recognizes, as he said, that we have a long way to go and that there is much to be done. There is no way that any of us want to see the various associations of Indian people held back because of the problems of two or three groups.
I am encouraged that a committee of this House can produce positive reports with all sorts of ideas for teacher training, hostels, university education, experiments in teacher training, co-operation with the provinces and the design of curricula to meet the requirements of the cultures involved. All this can be done and we are working toward it with the co-operation and assistance of all concerned on a basis which takes it beyond the field of partisanship. All this can and will be achieved.
Mr. Speaker, I say to the minister that we will continue to have our battles. We have had them before. I have won some and lost some. However, if he continues to show this kind of positive approach to resolving the problems of the Indian and Eskimo peoples of Canada and to working with them, I think we shall very shortly see the results of these programs and his work.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I think this speech will create some reverberations. As the minister was speaking I had before me a book which has recently been published, called "Touch of Earth," by a young woman named T. C. McLuhan. I should explain to the House that this is a compilation of speeches and statements made by leaders of the Indian peoples covering a span of time from the late 1700s until 1971. I read the following:
Our people no longer believe. It is that simple and it is that sad. The Canadian government can promise involvement, consultation, progressive human and economic development programs. We will no longer believe them-
After generations of endless frustration with the Canadian government, our people are tired and impatient. Before the Canadian government tries to feed us hypocritical policy statements, more empty promises, more forked tonguistics, our people want, our people, the Indians, demand just settlement of all our treaty and aboriginal rights. Fulfillment of Indian rights by the Queen's government must come before there can be any further co-operation between the Indians and the government. We demand nothing more. We expect nothing less.
Those words may be somewhat familiar to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. I have a strange feeling that although the minister was ostensibly addressing Your Honour, and through Your Honour the other members of the House, he was actually addressing many of his remarks to somebody who does not have a seat in the House at present. That is why I put on the record some of the words contained in this book. If the minister has not already identified their originator, let me tell him that they were written by a Cree Indian named Harold Cardinal who was born in 1945 in High Prairie, Alberta.
The year 1945 happens to be the year when I was first a candidate for election to Parliament. One of the things I vividly recollect hearing during that election campaign in one of the places I visited was that families whose girls were prepared to sleep with the representative of the Minister of Indian Affairs would get welfare, whereas families whose girls would not do that would not get welfare. At that time I resolved that if I were elected to Parliament, and even if I were not, I would do all I could to end that kind of gross human indignity. That year was not long ago. I freely concede that the attitude of many Canadians toward Indians who dwell within our borders has changed considerably since then. Perhaps the situa-
Indian Affairs
tion reported to me then can no longer be found within the length and breadth of our land: I certainly hope so.
If the minister is sincere, as I hope he is and as he certainly sounded this afternoon, he will recognize the import of the words saying that these things cannot be settled until there has been a just settlement of "our treaty and aboriginal rights". Those words tend to put in focus the report of the committee which is before us for discussion. It should be apparent to all members-and as a member of the committee who had some part in the drafting of the report I favour its adoption by the House- that the report ought to stimulate discussion. I hope the document will stimulate discussion and that it will lead people to search out new ideas. In my view that is all the committee basically intended with regard to the initial impact of the report.
The introduction to the statement in the book from which I have just quoted says that in the last several years he, Harold Cardinal, has become a skilful politician speaking out for Indian rights in Canada. The minister talked about politics. If the minister is suggesting that this subject is far too important for what is commonly described as narrow partisan politics, I agree with him. Certainly, all the members of the Indian affairs committee felt in approaching this report that narrow partisan politics had no place in their deliberations. In drawing up the report partisan politics was not a consideration. However, if the minister is discussing politics in a broader sense then I, for one, consider this to be one of the most important and vital political issues within our country today.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Right.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
It should be dealt with in this chamber in that light. In considering this report we are trying to come to grips with a fundamental question. I agree with the minister when he says that much still needs to be done to change the attitude and outlook of many non-Indian Canadians. As he suggested in his speech, there is a great need for this to happen in the province of Alberta. To judge from my brief exposure to the situation in the northeastern part of that province, the minister has put his finger on one of the facets of the problem there.
However, since the minister tried to imply in his speech today, as another hon. member on the other side of the House did, that there was virtually unanimous agreement in the House on the white paper, let me say again that the disagreement in this House was not so much about what was in the white paper as about what was not in it. That is why many Indian leaders of this country continue to distrust the government.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has said-and the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development has underlined what he said-that aboriginal rights per se do not exist in this country. That I challenge. Their existence is implicit if there is to be any successful outcome with regard to actions that may be taken to improve educational opportunities for the Indian people of Canada. Let us come to grips with the issue on that plane. Seen in that perspective, the recommendations in the committee report, or any discussion as to what was or was not in the white paper, become relatively unimportant, although I admit that these recommendations and discussions are

November 24, 1971
Indian Affairs
important. I say that because we live in an ongoing society. Young people are growing up and reaching the age when they want to enter into the fullness of our society as adults.
It is no light thing for young Indian people or for other young people of this country to lose one year's schooling. Let me say in this chamber, as I said in a memorandum I sent to members of the House shortly after visiting northeastern Alberta, that I listened to an earnest discussion taking place among a group of teenage children from that area. They discussed their personal situations and the struggle that was going on there. They said they would gladly sacrifice one year of their schooling if it would increase the chance of their younger brothers and sisters obtaining a better education. I admire those children for taking that position: I think they were right.
In his reference to that situation the minister overlooked the depth of understanding that young Indian people have of just what is involved in this whole question. Maybe they have some of the impatience of youth, perhaps a little of the kind of impatience of youth displayed by the minister in his speech this afternoon, even though they are a few years his junior. However, there does come that old cry that has been echoed throughout the ages, "How long, O Lord, how long?"
One should talk to the older Indian people who know what it was like 50, 60 or 75'years ago. He would then understand that in an age when there is a reawakening of understanding among Indian people of what they are and the way of life they enjoy, they become impatient. They are prepared to make sacrifices to see things happen. One member who participated in this debate referred to sections of the report. I agree with him that this is one of the key parts of the report. He quoted the following words:
In those schools remaining under the control of the educational branch, the committee believes that the objectives of the federal schools should be the creation of models of excellence which will furnish to Indian and Eskimo young people, an education which will provide to them equality of opportunity and the ability to be employed at every level of the economy of the regions in which they live.
That report was tabled in the House on June 30. Members will recall that the House recessed at the end of that sitting day and there was no opportunity for discussion of the report until the House returned in the fall. There was no opportunity for any immediate response from the government to the proposals of the report. I think all members of the committee will agree that we did not expect from the government a full-fledged reply or assessment of the proposals the next day or within the next week. The minister said in his speech-this was probably a slip-that only a couple of months have gone by. We are getting on toward the end of November. The report has been on the table since June 30. That is more than two months ago. Until today, the first response of the minister that apparently relates to the content of the report can be found in a speech that he made in Thunder Bay on September 17, when he said:
Is it not more sensible to make the provincial systems excellent for Indian, Metis and non-Indian students alike? Can we create an additional structure of expertise in a federal school system scattered across Canada?
That appears to be a response by the minister to the committee's recommendation. If I am wrong, the minister has the opportunity of correcting me. If one examines the phraseology, "Is it not more sensible to make the provincial systems excellent for Indians and Metis," perhaps one could retort that the obvious answer is that they should probably both become systems of excellence. If the text which I have is correct, the minister later said:
With the participation of the Indian community we are influencing the provincial systems. We fund the education and, as buyers of service, we can speak effectively to the provinces.
I suggest that statement requires considerable examination in light of the recommendations of the committee report and in light of some of the facts of the situation that some of us know. From time to time the minister has given us various statistics about the percentage of Indian people who are in the general school system, those remaining within the federal Indian school system and how this has been increasing.
I think I am correct when I say that the earliest move which brought Indian children in numbers into the general school system of a province took place in British Columbia. In the 1950s an agreement was made between the Indian affairs branch and one of the school boards in my constituency. This set up the formula, which still basically applies, of a pro rata, per capita grant and a pro rata allowance per pupil for Indian children attending school in a system run by a provincial school board. In that particular instance I think it was done with the knowledge and desire of the Indian people in the area. The tempo of that development increased rather rapidly in the province of British Columbia, as far as I know largely with the consent and in some cases at the request of the Indian people.
I suggest the basic reason for that happening in British Columbia in the way it did is that the Indian people had become fed up with the poor quality and ineptitude of the educational system administered by the Indian affairs branch. They were prepared to try any other possible alternative in order to help their children get a meaningful education. A great many Indian people in British Columbia today still feel that is probably the best arrangement in many localities, particularly where there are small Indian bands living fairly close to a non-Indian community.
I suggest that many of the Indians of British Columbia are now starting to question the desirability of that kind of arrangement. They are beginning to be concerned. This is partly because they are becoming aware of the value of their cultural heritage. They are becoming increasingly concerned that their children will be lost in the shuffle and that they will become little white men.
Concern was expressed to the committee by representatives from many parts of Canada. Many witnesses appeared before the committee. This report resulted from that accumulation of evidence. Despite the fact that the minister said we fund education and as buyers of service we can speak effectively to the provinces, I see very little tangible evidence that this is so in the province of British Columbia. There are some rather weak and fumbling moves being developed within the province which may, hopefully, bring about some enrichment of the provincial school curriculum so that it will include an opportunity

November 24, 1971

for both Indian and non-Indian children to acquire a true picture of the history of the Indian people and some knowledge of their culture and art. Such moves as are being made are pitifully few and increasingly difficult to equate with the real needs of Canadian society today and the growth and aspirations of the Indian people.
In British Columbia as well as in other parts of the country it is being argued that the white community is using this new education policy as a gimmick to divert federal funds into provincial schools for the benefit of non-Indian children. I was approached a year or two ago by a knowledgeable and sincere teacher employed in one of the schools in my constituency. He was concerned that money coming from the Department of Indian Affairs was not being used for the benefit of Indians but to provide fancier school facilities for non-Indian pupils. This question is being raised by many Indians in various parts of Canada, as the minister will find if he cares to listen-whether once again the white man with his ingenuity is not getting the benefit of funds made available by the department to provide better education for Indians.

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development

speechtext: If such a situation is developing, would it not be wise for the Indians to force the hands of provincial authorities to do things right, with the help of the federal government? If these funds are not being allocated in the best way possible, would it not be right for the Indians, together with us, to try to correct this by putting pressure on the provincial governments? Should we throw the whole system away because there may be some such shortcoming as the one to which the hon. member has referred?

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: That is a perfectly reasonable question. I agree efforts should be made to ensure that these funds are spent in the way in which they should be spent. But I had a recent report on a situation which arose in the province of New Brunswick, and the minister can check this out if he wishes. When demands are made by the Indian people in this area they are either ignored or foiled. The minister has referred to the fact that certain provinces allow representatives of the Indian people to sit on school boards. But as far as I know, they are in a minority, possibly with only one representative, and the Indians have no power as a minority of one on a school board. This is why, among other things, many of the Indian people are saying it would be much better, given all the circumstances of today, to have their own schools and their own school boards to operate them.

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development

speechtext: There are some.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The minister talks about putting pressure on provincial school systems. The committee in its consideration of this question felt that because of the realities of the situation in the various provinces one of the most effective ways of putting pressure on provincial school systems as far as excellence of programs is concerned would be to provide schools which would be models of excellence in certain appropriate locations-federal schools built and operated in the way the Indian people feel they should be and in the way in which the minister
Indian Affairs
says he wants them to be-so that the Indian people may be equal economically while still being free to remain Indians.

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: A question for clarification. Would it not be advisable to seek to get provincial laws amended to enable the Indians to appoint representatives to school board in proportion to their population? We can work in that direction. I do not think that because there is a problem we should turn back the clock.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: That, of course, is one of the fundamental questions raised in the committee report. Would we be turning back the clock if the Indian people feel this is what they need, if they feel that instead of fading out of the picture the minister's department should set an example for the rest of the country? This is the question which was raised in the report and it is one which has to be answered.

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: That is exactly what I am doing.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The committee report recommends-and perhaps it is in error:
1. That the government should continue its policy that no transfers of education programs from the federal level to provincial systems take place without the express and clear approval of the majority of the parents in each community concerned.

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: That is exactly the policy we are following now. There is no transfer without the agreement of the Indians.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: This was the assumption in the mind of members of the committee when they drafted this report. But let us consider what has happened since this report was laid on the table of the House on June 30. On September 17 the minister, in effect, challenged the assumption of the report. In the first instance, when the Indians clearly indicated that they did not want to go into the provincial school system, preferring to have their own school on their own reserves, the minister told the House, "It is physically impossible to build six schools in one year." Those are his own words. How much sense does that make in a country which possesses all the materials we could hope for? And the people who are not now working could build those schools.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: The minister says we cannot build six schools in one year. When the minister says we would be turning back the clock, this question arises in my mind-

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: On a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker, I should like to correct the impression the hon. member has given. I said I was not interested in building the schools because that was not the solution. The Indians of the Keecheewin are not asking me to build a high school there, nor is that what the others are asking really. They want a better system, and I think this can be achieved in the school they are attending right now.

The answer is no. The supplementary estimates themselves prove that. That is one side of the question, but the other and more fundamental part of the question is this. The minister is falling over the stumbling block of the refusal of his government to recognize aboriginal rights, to recognize that it is not a matter of a hand-out being made by Parliament, to recognize that we have been paying very cheap rent for this country for a long time and that it is about time we did something to rectify the situation.
I do not know whether to blame the minister or not. I am not privy to what goes on in cabinet and this has not yet been leaked. All I can go by is the statement made by the head of the government, who time and again has said "Perhaps we will have a look at treaty rights, but aboriginal rights, no".
