speechtext:
We are discussing the report of a committee on education and, hopefully, it will receive favourable consideration by the House as a whole. I have tried to answer all the questions that the minister has wanted to ask me, and in conclusion I would like to make a quick reference to the book to which I referred earlier. I think it is fundamental to the growth of the understanding that is required to recognize just what it is that we owe the Indian people. I am not now talking, as I was a moment ago, about what we may owe them for the use of the land that once was all theirs, but about something more important perhaps than even that. There is an introduction in this book entitled "The Spirit of the Earth". While it contains speeches from Indian people from various parts of North America, the book is written by a citizen of the United States. The introduction has this to say, among other things:
It is well understood that the only decent future for us who live in America now is through a rediscovery of our environment. We need to establish a right relationship with the land and its resources; otherwise, the destruction of the Indian will be followed by the destruction of nature; and in the destruction of nature will follow the destruction of ourselves.
(Mr. Barnett.]
November 24, 1971

The Indians, in a sense, knew this all along. For many generations they learned how to live in America, in a state of balance, or, as a Christian would say, in a state of grace. Perhaps now, after hundreds of years of ignoring their wisdom, we may learn from the Indians.

speakeroldname: Hon. Martin P. O'Connell (Minister of State):
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to go over the ground so eloquently covered by my colleague, the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien), earlier this afternoon. I was glad to hear him congratulate the members of the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development for its report on education. All of us will have an opportunity to hear from him again tomorrow and to put questions concerning the general situation that is being debated in the House this afternoon, as well as questions concerning education and grants that are in some dispute.
For my part, I have been a very interested and active observer of and participant in native affairs for a number of years, and in my view more solid progress has been achieved in three years than has been realized in the past several decades. This progress is evident not only in education. I am not one of those who sees education as the panacea for all problems, but when the minister is able to say, for example, that there has been a doubling of students at university level this year over last year and that there is increasing improvement throughout the educational system, then I think progress becomes evident.
No one would expect me to stand up in this House and say all is well, rosy and satisfactory. It is not. There is far too much still to be done. However, I believe if we are to be fair to the people of Canada we should try to keep in perspective that which is being done and that which has been done. I think it is only fair to say that more is being done with the help of this minister than in any previous period in our dealings with the native people. He is not a "yes" man, as he told us this afternoon. I believe he is a fair man and is energetic as no one else before him. He is direct, intensely human, and a dedicated minister. I wished to stand up and say this in the House of Commons because I have not always agreed with governments in the past and with ministers who have been handling this most complicated and exciting portfolio.
I think we should admit to ourselves-and I am not saying this is in a partisan manner-that this has been the first government in Canadian history to place such large resources, financial, technical and other, directly into the hands of the native people. This is the first government to have gone that route. Of course, this will lead to difficulties. It will lead to irritations and to many frictions. That is what we must expect.
Of course, controversial incidents will arise. They will arise because this very process of putting resources into the hands of people accelerates their social and economic development, accelerates the whole process that it sharpens everyone's visibility of the inequalities which exist and the injustices which remain. We all see this and we all experience it. In this accelerated process people are confronted with these things as never before. Nonetheless, the most useful thing this government has been able to do has been to hand these resources over to these people and
Indian Affairs
to express its general confidence that they can administer them well and that they will bring about the development which decades of programs and decades of good intentions have not been able to achieve.
As I say, we must expect that we will run into difficulties. I do not want to see this process slowed down. I do not believe it is being slowed down. We must iron out the difficulties as they arise in financial and administrative programs. If they arise in political activities we must iron them out. Certainly, for three years we have launched ourselves as a Parliament and as a government in a process of mutual confidence with the native people. But the government itself cannot complete this process without the full, equal and willing participation of the native people.
The development going on now is rapid enough that I believe we could describe it as explosive when seen in the longer perspective of history and in the longer perspective of the preceding years in the lives of people of native ancestry. However, the method which is being followed is the only sure way. The government has followed this path and I am confident it will stay on that path. It is the only sure way. The native people themselves have told us it is the only way and have sought it as the path to their self-fulfillment, that is, by having resources placed in their own hands.
I should like to pursue that thought a little further and say again that this will present grave difficulties from time to time. This is what we will have to learn to live with while correcting them. The sure way to self-fulfillment, to equality, to justice is through social development, through economic development and through cultural development programs by having resources oneself. This is true because the people then become involved in unfolding their own destiny. They become involved not only in the sense of personal commitment-this is important in itself to release energies-but also as communities and as groups with a very strong communal sense of identity and with a long history and heritage.
It is the sure way because having resources in one's own hands gives people the confidence that the change they are negotiating will not bring about cultural disappearance and will not be the end of the road for the long human history of native culture and experience in North America. In my view, many of the weaknesses in the past in programs, in projects, in expenditures and in respect of high hopes have arisen because programs were delivered to a relatively passive group of people who sheltered sometimes from them for fear that involvement would mean the end of their heritage and that they would go into a stream and disappear. No people in history ever willingly do that.
We would not want to feel, and no cultural group of any origin in Canada would want to feel, that its future was one of disappearance. They want to feel there is a secure place for persons of all heritages to work out a destiny here in this free land. That assurance, in the case of the Indian people, and because of the long history of distrust and because of the long route they have had to travel, can be given only by turning over to them major financial resources and responsibilities. This can be done with confidence provided that between us we can and will work out the procedures that will enable us as a responsible

November 24, 1971
Indian Affairs
Parliament to evaluate programs and to be accountable for the funds and to enable responsible organizations to develop programs which the native people feel will succeed.
This can be accomplished only through a course of consultation and mutual trust. Consultation has taken place between the native organizations, the native communities, the native people and this government in a degree never before realized. 1 think if we want to keep things in perspective and be fair, we will all admit this. Consultations began on the Indian Act. They came to an end with the publication of a policy paper containing features the Indian people did not like. Too much emphasis, perhaps, was placed on legal equality and too little on social and economic development without which legalisms mean nothing. So that paper was set aside by the government as well as by the native people and a new process of consultation and the transfer of major resources to them began to take place.
What are some of the transferred resources about which I am speaking? I should like to mention just a few. There is a funding program known as core funding. I will come back to that later. There is the discussion that has taken place on educational cultural centres, and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has indicated in his speech on mul-ticulturalism that the government is taking steps to make funds available to assist native organizations to establish these cultural educational centres. This is one of the soundest and most hopeful concepts that has arisen over the past few years and I for one am satisfied and confident that we will see a major social, cultural and economic transformation take place through the medium of these educational cultural centres.
Another area is the economic development grants from the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. Most of us know that the first major grant happened to have been made in Alberta to the Blood reserve. It was in the order of $650,000 to $700,000, to assist a native company on that reserve to develop a major manufacturing facility for sectional and mobile homes.
It was a very hard struggle to put all the pieces together. They were put together with the maximum amount of effort on the part of this government, on the part of the Alberta Indian Association and on the part of the reserve people. It was made to work and, if my memory is correct, the project is working. There is a completely new spirit on that reserve and new urban developments are taking place. The first couple of years' production has been sold in advance. This is a piece of evidence that when native people themselves have the resources and the opportunity, they seize it as well as any other group in this country and they can administer and bring about significant economic, social and community developments of which they can be proud and we too can be proud with them.
I will not go into the economic side any further, although one could quote many examples. There are many new opportunities through revised five-year federal-provincial ARDA agreements specifically designed for the opportunities they can give to people of native ancestry.
(Mr. O'Connell.]
Before coming back to core funding I should mention the funds which this government has made available to native organizations so that they can engage their own professional counsel to consider the matter of treaty rights with the understanding that the federal government will consider these questions jointly and will negotiate, through some joint mechanism, this long and troubled matter in our common history.
Now I should like to say a few words about core funding since I think it is fairly basic to the point I am trying to make about the transfer of governmental resources to non-governmental bodies to enable them to engage in important activities in social and cultural development. Core funding is a program agreed to by the government some months ago to rationalize a system that had been developing for two or three years of making grants to native organizations.
Currently, I believe between 20 and 26 native organizations are receiving substantial sums of money which in their total come to several million dollars so that they can maintain their organizations through which they can then seek project or program funds from other departments of the federal government or from provincial funding departments and agencies or from private sources. These core funding arrangements are on a formula basis. They enable these Indian, Metis and Eskimo associations to have full-time staff, depending on certain variables between the provinces and territories, ranging between six to twelve persons for each association-permanent staff without which they cannot be expected to maintain the developmental process on which they are so keen. For the first time, through the decision of this government, they can have an assured ongoing permanent staff. This is a major transfer of resources. It goes further. They can have not only staff but they are provided with funds for office expenses so that a central office can be maintained with secretaries and equipment.
Also, additional funds are provided for travel expenses for those workers on the core staff, together with additional funds for executive meetings so that persons in their constituency around the province can come to consult. Additional funds are also provided for an annual meeting. Funds are made available to enable these associations to obtain professional and technical advice from persons chosen by themselves. The core funding program of this federal government covers these expenditure items on an ongoing basis so that these organizations can have an assured existence while they do their work.
The concept goes to the next step and recognizes that the communities in the field scattered around the province need to relate to their associations just as the central bodies need to have their grass-roots communications and support. Hence, the core funding includes additional funds for up to 12 persons depending on the variables in the provinces. We could call these additional staff persons communications workers or field workers, if that is a more understandable phrase. So there is the staff in the central office and there are communications workers to keep in touch with the field so that those communities can have a voice in the programs that their associations develop.
These associations are democratically elected. They represent those people and they have facilities to go back

and forth from the field to the organizations to develop their programs in their own best interest. I think this is a most important development in the relationship between the government, this Parliament and the people of Canada in general and our native people. Assistance goes not only to Indians as defined under the Indian Act; this assistance is available to non-status Indians and to Metis and Eskimos in Canada, so that today some 26 or so associations are receiving this kind of support on an assured basis, one that they have never had before which enables them to participate and consult.
Few weeks go by without an airplane bringing to Ottawa delegations of these native organizations to continue this consultative process. Few weeks go by in which officials of various departments of the government are not on other airplanes going into the field in the provinces to carry on this consultative process.
The basic concept of core funding goes yet a further step and I would like to describe it. It puts those organizations which are representing the native peoples into a position where they can seek program funds from various departments and no longer are confined to a single department of the government. It puts them in a position to go on to another department, or another or another, like any other citizen of Canada. It opens up the whole range of government services to native people in a way that has not been opened before.
That is one of the most important and heartening developments of the last three years, since it confirms the conviction of this government that the native people want to be on a footing of equality with all other citizens in this country and wish to have opened to them the whole range of services, not only of this government but of all other levels of government and have access equally to the private sector.
I want to conclude with just a brief reference to the importance the government sees in what for lack of a better phrase I am going to call the question of culture. There is no secure social development without recognition that it takes place through a process that we have to call a cultural process. We know this now and all over the world it is known. If there is any experience that has become common to all of us through the United Nations in the social and economic field, it is surely the knowledge that development is a cultural process. If people do not feel secure on the cultural front, they hang back and will not go into the kind of social change that is taking place all over the world today, and into the economic process that brings such rapid social change in its train.
Indian Affairs
The point that I am coming to, Mr. Speaker, is that the cultural educational centre is a recognition of the cultural dimension. The developments that the minister has already pointed to in self-administration in the field of education also confirm that interest in the cultural process, so that native people will feel that the educational process also gives room for those cultural concerns without which they do not want to go down that path of development.
The final point I want to make on the cultural side is that the core funding, if it does anything at all, says to the native people through their organizations, "Here are resources with which you yourselves can develop the kind of programs, social, economic and educational that you feel will allow this development to take place without threatening, without challenging, without undermining the cultural continuity which you, and we too, want to see assured."
What in effect is happening in a short period of time is that the native peoples of Canada-I include the Metis people and the Eskimos in this summary statement-are making the greatest turning point in their history, and we too are part of that turning point. If I could use a metaphor, it is as if we are all standing together on a shoreline where we are negotiating social, cultural and economic changes. And I am convinced that the generations that follow ours, looking at these changes that are taking place today, will find many footprints on that shoreline and among them, well in the forefront, they will find the footprints of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development.
